utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. There is a ruling the Chamber wishes to issue at this stage. On 14th of June, 2011, the Chamber ordered the Prosecution to file public redacted versions of six witness statements which had been previously admitted under seal by the Chamber pursuant to Rule 92 bis. On 27th of June, 2011, the Prosecution filed a notification of compliance with the Trial Chamber's order in relation to witness statements admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis, requesting the Chamber to admit into evidence the public redacted version of the witness statements, which have now been up-loaded into e-court and bear 65 ter numbers 08874A, 12138A, 90137A, 90138A, 90139A and 90140A. The Chamber has reviewed these six documents and will admit them into evidence. The Chamber, therefore, requests the Registry to assign exhibit numbers to these documents. Unless there's any matter to deal with in the absence of the witness, let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to alert the Chamber and the parties that the next witness, there's an outstanding motion for disclosure of ex parte materials concerning the protective measures, and we would like to have that material before the beginning of the cross-examination of the next witness, if we are to receive that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do we have the response to that motion referred to by Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You should have received it yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll check it after this session. Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After everything we looked at yesterday, you also had problems with the law and with the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when or where. I didn't have any problems. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D3639.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you interviewed on the 22nd of July, 1994, at the MUP of the Republic of Serbia? Was this interview conducted with you by the police because, as we can see in the first paragraph -- can we please see the next page, page 3 in English -- because this person whom you took from Bijeljina to Belgrade had a forged personal identification card with him? The fact that Edib owned a falsified ID -- [In English] "Edib owned a falsified ..." [Interpretation] And here in Serbian, you can see the fact that Edib owned a falsified ID card in the name of Zoran Jovanovic, and so on and so forth, "I didn't know." Was this interview conducted with you at the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they conducted an interview with me at the Serbian police because Edib was in my apartment. I had brought him from the hospital in Bijeljina, or, rather, from Lopare, where he was accommodated when he was taken from the veterinary station in Bijeljina. He was a veterinary [as interpreted], himself, and he was accommodated at the dressing room of the Lopare Football Club. And through some connections, I took him out of there, I put him in a car and I brought him to Belgrade. I took him for treatment to the Military Medical Academy, where he stayed for a while because he had serious injures of his kidneys and other injuries that he had sustained because he was hit. He also had a hematoma. The police which came to check if he was there, brought him in and then found a forged personal ID card on him. I didn't know this and I wasn't interested in it. He probably wanted to have something just in case his ID was checked so that he wouldn't be identified as a Muslim, and that was probably the reason he had this on him. This is what he told me later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you tell us how this is relevant to your case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness was a policeman with the Federal SUP, and his colleagues called him to have an interview with him because he had a man with a forged ID and who had entered Serbia illegally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but how is this relevant, either in relation to your case or in relation to the evidence given in his examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution would not have any objections to this because it actually confirms the evidence that the witness has given. So that would be the relevance, as the Prosecution would see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have established that this witness was dismissed from the police, that the police often had suspicions against him, that he was often questioned, and that he was sent away from Bijeljina because he over-stepped his authority. And this creates a full picture of this witness, not just from the point of view of credibility, but, generally speaking, it shows that he is not fit to be a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1406, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that Mr. Karadzic says is completely untrue, and it has nothing to do with reality. I was officially retired. I did not have any problems. It's normal that the service should take information from me about circumstances connected with Edib. I'm proud that I was in a situation to help this man and other people. I'm not ashamed of that at any moment. On the contrary, this confirms that whatever I say is the truth. And I was not dismissed from service. I was retired with all the entitlements that are due to any member of the Federal Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were sent away from Bijeljina, Mr. Davidovic, from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a different subject. I completed my mandate when the SDS and the SDA had me replaced. That is to say, two other persons were assigned to my position in Bijeljina, according to a decision, because they belonged to the party, first, of the chief, Predrag Jesuric, and then he replaced me. And the other position of commander was for the SDA. A teacher was appointed to that position. I didn't know him at all. I was not thrown away, but I was sent on holiday and I needed to wait for my new assignment. And in the meantime, this was finished even before I was in a situation to be replaced, I received an offer to be transferred to the Federal SUP. I communicated with them. They said they approved of my transfer. And when I was thrown out from Bijeljina, as you say, then there was an Assembly decision. When I got there in 1992 and when I did what I did, that is to say, I disarmed paramilitaries, because the first thing I did when I came to Bijeljina, I arrested members of Arkan's units or they fled from Bijeljina, to the last man. Later on, I found a group of five of them in a house. They were looting during the night in Bijeljina. Later on, when I arrested the murderers of Salko Hukic, and when the curfew was imposed by the command and the corps commander, Colonel Ilic, then, during the night, we arrested Mauzer and brought him to the SUP. And after that, there was hue and cry after me. They said that I was a Communist, that I had come there to arrest people again and to re-institute the old regime. And then there was a request that proceedings be initiated against me before the Assembly and that I should be sent away from the territory of the municipality. But the decision was not carried out because I continued working in Brcko after that, and then in Zvornik, and then once again in Bijeljina. And the decision that was made just confirms that when I came there, I worked in accordance with the law, rightfully, and that the Crisis Staff didn't like me, and so did the others who were doing improper things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, what you described, you were commended for what you did, and you were confirmed both by the representatives of the government, I mean the Miskin one who came from Pale to commend you, and also the deputies and other imminent people from Bijeljina. In 1992, you were thrown away when you over-stepped your authority and when you did things which were outside of the law. This is what I'm talking about. And for what you now describe, weren't you commended and confirmed for that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Assembly meeting, Jovo Miskin was present, and throughout the time he was there with me, and he was informed about everything that was happening. At that Assembly meeting, he spoke several times about the measures I took and what I was doing in order to prevent the mistreatment of Muslims and everything else that had been happening up to my arrival. Except in addition to Jovo Miskin and what he said, and what other deputies said, the majority of the SDS members voted for a decision requesting that I should be expelled from the Bijeljina territory. Savo Kujic, who was the SDS secretary at the time, even requested that I should be prohibited from coming to Bijeljina. However, I'm not sure if the decision was adopted. Everything that they requested could not affect me, nor could they make a decision to dismiss me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, to cut a long story short, Jovo Miskin is a government representative who had come from Pale, was supporting you all along; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you were doing, that is to say, you arrested paramilitaries and criminals, is something you did on the order of Momo, who -- of me. I was the president of the SDS and the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the orders of Mico Stanisic. Whether you informed Mico Stanisic about that, I don't know, but Mico Stanisic told me that we should come to help with disarming the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have the last paragraph of this statement which you gave to the Serbian MUP: "Bearing in mind ..." This is the last paragraph we see on the English page. "Bearing in mind that ..." We can see it there in English, we can start: "Bearing in mind that between April and September 1992, at the order of the Republika Srpska leadership, I participated in the identification and capture of Serbian war criminals and the disarming of various Serbian paramilitary formations, and the fact that since 1992, I have been receiving frequent threats from members of these groups, I conclude that this was provocation ..." And so on and so forth. So didn't you clearly confirm to them here that you were aware that the leadership of Republika Srpska requested you to make these arrests and to disarm the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anything else. You and Mico Stanisic and his deputy, they are the leaders. They are the leadership of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 149 of your statement, you said: "After I left Bijeljina in August 1992, the SDS reorganised itself, and new people were appointed ..." And so on and so forth. Let us establish, when did you leave Bijeljina? The first line and the first sentence of paragraph 149 is what I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Bijeljina sometime in the second half of July, I think, or in mid-July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were not in Bijeljina in September; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was in Pljevlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please have a look at paragraph 150. You say that after these new people were appointed, they made a plan for the ethnic cleansing of Muslims, those that remained in Bijeljina, Lopare and Zvornik. There were still around 17.000 Muslims in Bijeljina and 12.000 Muslims in Janja: "This plan was discussed in front of me in the corridor of the Executive Council offices." So after you had left, the SDS was consolidated, and the new leadership made a plan and discussed about it in front of you, even though you had left. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I talked about the changes that happened after I had left and that there was new leadership in Bijeljina who were appointed to specific positions at the Bijeljina MUP. When you say that I was present, what I had in mind and what I said was that I was present at the Crisis Staff or the particular council which made decisions and reviewed the security situation while I was in Bijeljina, and I was personally present when they adopted the plan which concerned the way they would work and how they should move out Muslims from Bijeljina. I remember well the decision in which they requested, as the first item --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait, wait. We'll reach that. Did the Crisis Staff exist in Bijeljina while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did. The chief of the Crisis Staff was Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report this, which you heard, to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed the federal minister in writing about that, because hey sent me to this area. I had also told Mico Stanisic about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we have this report of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not have a chance to see it. No one offered it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then here in paragraph 50, you list quite a number of men who, in your view, made these plans for ethnic cleansing of Bijeljina, in which in August or after August, there were still 17.000 Muslims, as well as 12.000 Muslims in Janja. And then you said that Moco Stankovic made a list, and after that this was carried out via Mauzer and the Security Service. You say that the leadership of Bijeljina made a list of Muslims who should be expelled and that this was carried out through Mauzer and the Security Service; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in order to clarify this, you have to allow me to tell you what was the reason for making such lists. As soon as the Serbian Democratic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, you said all that in your statements. I want to clarify what I'm interested in. I'm leading the cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, do you have your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you must have referred to 150, not 50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 150, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on, you say that Drago Vukovic was a member of the Crisis Staff and the chief of the Security Service and the Public Security Station; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, State Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say how a family was killed. This is item 151. First of all, the plan which was made and carried out through Mauzer and the Security Services, was that something you reported to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Who could I report that to? To those who were doing this and making the lists? Who can you report it to? This was information which I submitted to my minister about the entire situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does not the police report this to the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever I found that there was some illegal act committed in Bijeljina, I would submit a criminal report, and there is -- there are records about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was happening after I had left Bijeljina and when the SUP was consolidated because they wanted to prevent the continuing peace in Bijeljina; namely, when I got there and when Muslims were not taken away anymore, when there was no more looting and killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they wanted to make chaos in their own house; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, precisely. That was the goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, you say that a family was killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The interpreters are having a terribly difficult task. Neither of you are leaving any breaks between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that then a Muslim family was killed, and that's paragraph 151: "On the opposite side of town, another family of 18 were killed." You also say this was done by Dusko Malovic's group. They killed a family of 18 from Bijeljina. He gave the orders to his men to do the killings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence of this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from Pljevlja in October, I was at Bosanska Villa together with Dusko Malovic because a meeting was supposed to be held there. Before the meeting, I had a chance to sit next to Dusko and ask him, Dusko, what happened in Bijeljina, who murdered that family, the Sarajlic family? And he said, Don't ask me anything about that. It was done at the request of the Security Service and their chief, Drago Vukovic. He personally told me that, and I stated that here at the Tribunal and also at the service where I worked, this information I learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you arrest him or report him because he was in Belgrade, in Serbia, at the time, and you were working for the Federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't arrest him, and I couldn't report him to SUP because the event took place in Bijeljina and he was in Belgrade all this time. And when this happened, Dusko Malovic was not in Bijeljina, but rather in Belgrade. He told me that his unit had done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. And when did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at some point in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the last two sentences of paragraph 151. The killings occurred in late September 1992. It was common knowledge that Malovic was responsible; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone in Bijeljina was saying at the time that they saw members of his group, because they wore a typical uniform and they were easy to recognise because of that. Everyone said that Dusko Malovic's men had done that. But I was not in Bijeljina at the time, and I didn't know that, nor could I inquire about details. The first information I reached was from Dusko in Belgrade once I had returned from Pljevlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 152. You say Malovic and his men also killed another family of three a few days in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What are the last names of these families; Sarajlic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one family, Sarajlic, and the other one is Sejmenovic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And third one is Malagic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly Malagic. I cannot remember all the names exactly. But it was Sarajlic. I know them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During another questioning, you said that you don't know anything about that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying. What do you mean, I don't know anything?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number that Mr. Karadzic referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3143 -- 3643. 3643.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor's Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 14th of January, 2008, question you about these incidents? Can we have an answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in my life did I give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the BH, nor do I know of this statement. And I would like to see whether there's a signature of mine on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what it says here: "On the 10th of January, 2008, in accordance with an agreement reached with Prosecutor Bozidarka Dodik, I conducted an interview with Milorad Davidovic, nicknamed Mico, born" et cetera, et cetera, "who according to certain information at the time of the disappearance of the families Sejmenovic, Sarajlic and Malagic, who was in Bijeljina as a member of the federal SUP." The transcript is full of shortcomings, and I'm sure that I'm to be blamed. This is what it says: "According to some information received when the families of Sejmenovic, Sarajlic and Malagic disappeared, he was in Bijeljina as a member of the Federal SUP."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person allegedly had an interview with me about all these things that are mentioned here. At the moment these families were killed, Sejmenovic, Sarajlic and Malagic, I was not in Bijeljina. I had left Bijeljina and went to Pljevlja. And the person who wrote up this note, saying that he or she had interviewed me, I do not recall this. It must have been an informal conversation. I probably didn't even want to go into any details. And it's not that I focused on what was actually happening at the time. I don't know who this person is, so why would I have this kind of discussion? Also, this detail that says that I was chief of the Public Security Station in Bijeljina, I think that has nothing to do with the time when I was there. So this doesn't make any sense, but, well, anybody can write up whatever they thought they learned as the member of a department or a service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It doesn't say here that you were chief. It says here that as a member of the Federal SUP, you were in Bijeljina at the time. Can we now have page 2. Look at paragraph 3: "Specifically as regards the perpetrators of the crime against the members of the Sejmenovic, Sarajlic and Malagic families, he does not know anything, except that retired policeman Miladin Vasilic knows more about that ..." And so on and so forth. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, and I say that once again. I cannot speak about what happened at the moment when the crime was committed, because I wasn't there at the time, but I did say that this policeman, Miladin Vasilic, should be interviewed because he was working at the time and he knew more about this. I think I said that and that it was recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Boze Bagaric is the investigator on the next page. So can we have the next page, please. And the prosecutor who ordered this interview is Bozidarka Dodik. We saw that on the first page, but can we see the last page. Sorry, while we're on this page anyway, you say that some person, Stevanovic, was part of my personal detail. You say that allegedly, in all fairness.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where it says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's underlined. Did you say that this person, Laura, was a security man of mine?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You proposed here a second stage of the investigation plan and who they should talk to. And can we have the last page now just to see who the signatory is. Investigator Boze Bagaric; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you answer the question asked by the accused? Mr. Davidovic, do you remember talking to or being interviewed by this investigator, Boze Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that some person - I don't know his name - came, and my impression was that this was not official, that this was an informal conversation, because this was a colleague who used to work in the service and we knew each other from earlier on. When I talked to him, I suggested to him that, among others, he talk to some people who were still in the service, like Vasilic, who was still in the service, the chief of the Public Security Service in Bijeljina, and that they try to talk to people who were closer to the actual events to see how it happened, how come these crimes were committed. He wrote this up as a note, and I cannot remember some of these things that he mentions here. But I really do not see anything controversial in this official note. Quite simply, he is providing information that was important to him, that was of interest to him. I am suggesting to him what should be done, and I'm saying that I'm not aware of any details of what was going on, that I was not there. But I know full well that this family was killed, and I know what the reason was; to create this atmosphere of fear, and hopelessness, and everything else that was happening in Bijeljina before I went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have a basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1407, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A few times you mentioned Mr. Drago Vukovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have a translation, and it's -- maybe Mr. Karadzic made a mistake. According to the binder that I have, it is under 3642, and it's with a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter, whereas I had a 1D number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We'll send the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that had been admitted in full. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Drago Vukovic, head of the National Security Service. Through this service, evacuations were carried out, or expulsions, and let's see what Mr. Vukovic says about that. Before that, let me ask you: Do you know that after Dayton, every public official had to go through very thorough clearance by the international community?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Drago Vukovic was, in the post-Dayton period, an adviser in the Joint Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D3637. This is the statement that was given by Mr. Drago Vukovic in 2005. And could we please have page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see what he says here. Everyone can see it. I don't need to read it. So he claims that we did not have any lists whatsoever, especially not lists of rich Muslims. And then he says further on that there were no organised expulsions of non-Serbs, and that many people, some of them highly-respectable citizens, led a normal life, some of them were members of the Army of Republika Srpska, and the majority Muslim population in Janja lived an absolutely normal life all the way up to 1994. It was that year that a large number of Muslims voluntarily left Janja and went to third countries. After the armed conflict, to the present day, most of them returned to their original place of residence. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know part of this, but I have to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please don't explain anything. Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He should be allowed to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course, of course. Please go on -- carry on, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No matter how hard I try to respond to Mr. Karadzic's questions, he doesn't allow me to do that. He just says, Tell me whether you know or not. Drago Vukovic wrote up a statement in which he says, inter alia, that it was peaceful in Bijeljina and that there were no lists. So who took these Muslims away, on the basis of what? How come they conducted the selection as to who was supposed to leave and who was not supposed to leave? Why did he not mention some of these highly-respectable citizens who stayed in Bijeljina? Out of 25.000 Muslims, only 5.000 remained in Bijeljina. Where are these Muslims? How were they brought together, how were they taken away? I know for sure, and I can confirm that, that Drago Vukovic was present during the night when families were being taken away, even people who were screaming on trucks, saying, Drago, please, give me some water. He just kept silent, and he pretended not to know these people and simply didn't want to intervene. Now, were there any lists? Yes, there were lists. They were made by local leaders of the SDS. And according to these lists, locally made, people were taken away. Some people managed to purchase their freedom. Others did not. So why did they voluntarily leave Janja in 1994, as Drago Vukovic said? How did that happen all of a sudden?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We've been given an explanation of that. Let me just ask you now, Mr. Davidovic: Since they left, there must have been some lists. This conclusion of yours, that there were lists, do you draw that on the fact that some persons left Bijeljina and Janja?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an opportunity of seeing a great many people who forcibly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether that is the conclusion you draw. You said [indiscernible] just now. Of course there must have been a lists, where are these people otherwise? Is this by way of an analogy that you are drawing this conclusion that there must have been a list because some people left?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, a list did exist because the Muslims themselves knew that they were on some kind of list. So for example, they went to see Moco Stankovic or some other prominent individuals in Bijeljina and they asked to be taken off these lists. And I had opportunity of seeing these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order for us to have a transcript, you have to slow down and put a pause between the question and answer. It's simply impossible. Mr. Davidovic, could you repeat your answer? Nothing has been noted after you said: "Well, look ..." Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim, with full responsibility and certainty, that the lists that were made in Bijeljina were made by the chiefs of the local SDS branches, and they were provided to the central service of Drago Vukovic, or someone else, who had these lists, or Vojkan Djurkovic, since I know that these lists existed, because some persons who were on these lists told me that they were on these lists, and then by resorting to financial resources, they managed to get their names off these lists. And some were not taken away because they managed, through these local officials in the local commune, to be able not to be taken away. And then in 1993 and 1994, people were gathered en masse and taken away, but I'm talking about the initial period when the Crisis Staff and the SDS started functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in this statement, paragraph 150 something -- 150 or 51, didn't you say it was done through the Security Service and Mauzer? Now you say that Drago Vukovic and the National Security Service instrumentalised Vojkan. So what do you stand by?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said earlier on. Lists were made, and they were provided to certain persons. I think they were provided to Drago Vukovic and Mauzer, who was head of the Crisis Staff in Bijeljina, who knew all about this and was taking care of all this. And this list and the names of persons who should be taken away are provided to Vojkan Djurkovic by someone, Vojkan Djurkovic who is the one who actually does this on the ground, corralled all the Muslims in Bijeljina. In the beginning, in 1992, and later on, these lists were not even necessary because Muslims were being taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say "I think"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim. I claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here in line 5, you say: "I think they were provided to Drago Vukovic." Right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm saying, I'm saying based on facts that I heard. I visited Drago Vukovic in his office. I saw other people as well. I had the opportunity of seeing the lists and many other things that nobody ever asked me about or is recorded in a statement. I had occasion to see many things. There's no reason for me to think one thing and say another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at 152, the end of 152, where you claim there was a plan to liquidate a group of Muslims, et cetera, et cetera. You say: "Through a public statement of Mirko Blagojevic, it was announced on all the radios." And then you say: "After that incident, the MUP of Republika Srpska issued a statement signed by Mr. Tomo Kovac, condemning that crime. It is not true that in those critical days, I used to see Dusko Malovic, who spent most of his time in Belgrade. On the day in question, I was not in Bijeljina . This is a perfidious lie by Prosecution witnesses, and Dusko Malovic is no longer alive to say otherwise." Is it true that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was killed in 1993. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the question you just asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say Drago Vukovic has nothing to do with it. He was a person who worked in the Security Service, and that he knows Dusko Malovic, and says that the latter spent most of his time in Belgrade. I know that he spent his time with Mico Stanisic and was accountable to him. But whenever Dusko -- but whenever Minister Mico Stanisic visited, Dusko made contact with him, and he talked to all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's going to be the fate of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When asked about this statement of Mr. Vukovic, you said: "I know part of this, but I have to explain." When you say you knew part of this, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the killings of these people or you mean the conversation with Dusko Malovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the statement of Vukovic, what he stated in this statement. What you meant is that you knew the incident or you knew --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we have any basis to admit this document, Mr. Karadzic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, also objection from the Prosecution side, because this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what I said, that I would not admit it, so your assistance is not necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D3670.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a record of witness interview, the witness being Momcilo Djilas, regarding the murder of Sarajlic, Sejmenovic and Malagic families on 24th/25th September 1992. Can we see page 3. It seems to be the second page in English. Page 2 in English. No, no, sorry, page 4 in English. Please look at the last fifth in Serbian: "I did not inquire any further into this incident because at that time it was very dangerous to inquire about such incidents. I emphasise this because at that time in the area of Bijeljina, there were special police units." It's page 5 in English. "... special police units, and I remember, in particular, members of such police who were natives of Sokolac and who had characteristic camouflage, black-and-white uniforms. I remember them because we police officers were in awe of them and we feared them all. We had to stand still even when they were just passing by us. I know they were subordinated to Dragan Andan and Mico Davidovic, and they did whatever they pleased in Bijeljina. On one occasion, there was a lineup of all members of active-duty and reserve policemen from Bijeljina ..." Can we have the next page in Serbian. "... on the street that connects the CSB and the traffic police. After we were lined up, Dragan Andan read out some sort of dispatch requesting assistance in Ugljevik because Muslims had allegedly almost taken control of Ugljevik. Then Andan said that those who don't want to go to the front-line should go to the barracks." And then further down, it says: "I emphasise that during the police line-up, Mico Davidovic was present. While we were standing, lined up, members of the Special Police Unit yelled from windows, calling us cowards and other names. I noted this incident especially because I know Andan and Davidovic gave orders to this Special Police Unit, their superiors. I also want to say that I am prepared to repeat this in court and to confront all those people who held back or lied about certain events." So this police officer, Momcilo Djilas, gave a statement in 2006 in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Agency for Protection and Investigations, and he says you were in Bijeljina in September, that you were the commander of that special unit, that regular policemen were in fear of you, and that you were present at this line-up. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain this. When I came to Bijeljina and when the Republic MUP assigned me -- assigned Dragan Andan to be a co-ordinator between me and the federal ministry, I did not know the unit of Dusko Malovic and they were not in Bijeljina. That unit came 10 days later and made their headquarters in the SUP of Bijeljina. The orders on their arrival and accommodation was issued by Mico Stanisic. This unit, which had its deputies and assistants, was subordinated only to Mico Stanisic. Dusko even told me that I have no right to command that unit, they have their own superiors, I have nothing to do with them, and they have completely different missions. As far as I know, and you can ask Dragan, who, by the way, already testified about this, and you will find out that I had no need of such a unit. I didn't need them for any operation because that unit had very heavy weaponry, and, as such, I did not need them, I did not need them with me. That's one thing. And the second thing about this line-up, I have to tell you the details. Considering that in the SUP of Bijeljina, in the Security Centre, there were over 1300 reserve policemen, everyone who wanted to keep away from the front-line, everybody who didn't want to be mobilised into the army, took refuge in the reserve police; that is, sons, rich tradesmen, people who were city people, who didn't want to go to the front-line. On one day, we decided to check how prepared they really were to be engaged somewhere actively, if necessary, and we made this test order, a fake order, saying that there was shooting in Majevica and that volunteers were necessary to go to the front-line to defend it. Out of a thousand men lined up there, the entire MUP came out into this street, 150 men only stepped out, 100 of them being regular policemen whose superior I was. Everyone else tried to skivvy and to avoid going to the front-line. And I told them then to leave their weapons, not to carry their weapons through town, and I said the entire unit, 800 men, should be given to the corps, and the others should not remain on the reserve police force because they were not necessary. And then chaos started. People cried, begged, but we remained firm that nobody can be amnestied from this. They were assigned to be on standby for defence efforts, not reserve police officers. And when I left in the second half of July, a good part of these reserve policemen returned, because I already told you who these were; people who had money; that is, sons, children of public officials, people who didn't want to go to the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this line-up took place in September. Now you told us that you left Bijeljina in the second half of July, but you were in Bijeljina in September, because this policeman was mobilised into the reserve police force only in September, and only after that mobilisation was he part of this lineup.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At least according to the translation that we have, the witness Djilas was speaking of September 1991 and not 1992. But there may be a mistake in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you clarify, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That could not have happened in September of that year. That was in early July 1992. And at the end of the day, there are documents at the SUP, when policemen were assigned to the army, to be at the disposal of the army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 3 in Serbian, page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't it written here, Mr. Davidovic, that he was mobilised in September 1992, and that, of course, he could have been present at that line-up only after being mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say when he was mobilised. I cannot confirm any dates he mentioned. All I know is when things happened. I say, with full responsibility, that it was in early July or perhaps the end of June, but that whole scene with the reserve force when we threw 800 men out of the reserve police force was not in September, because beginning with the second half of July, I was in Pljevlja, doing something completely different for the federal ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see now September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, and this witness is only speaking about when he was mobilised. When this event took place that he described, there's no date at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, together with Andan, you were present at this line-up. Andan was the superior of this unit, and you were working together with him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan was a co-ordinator between the MUP of Republika Srpska and me, as a member of the Federal Ministry of Internal Affairs. With this kind of organisation, Dragan was re-assigned to become the chief of the Security Centre in Bijeljina. Concerning the unit that was at my disposal, he could not have been subordinated to me. Whether he was the subordinate of the chief of the centre in Bijeljina, I don't know. But Dusko Malovic told me before that Mico Stanisic said, I can't allow anyone else to have command over this unit, and I'm sorry, because I know you well, I can't allow even you to command over this unit. Everything done with them is strictly between me and Mico Stanisic, the minister. And that was the end of that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate shorter answers whenever possible. So you say you did not have command over that unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 7497, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from July 1992, the 4th of July. General Tolimir, who was a colonel at the time, is writing about the case when you over-stepped your authority. He says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic should give us a reference where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This first paragraph says you were there with that unit. In the second paragraph: "The Eastern Bosnian Corps Command of the Army of SR BH has faced the following problems with the activities of that MUP special unit: over-stepping of authority vis-a-vis military officials; abuse of authority; disrespect of military and police patrols; searches of the military and other vehicles, even the military police vehicles and intelligence and security authorities' vehicles; arrests of military officials, while Mico Davidovic, the commander of the unit, is behind all of these activities." And then paragraph 4 says: "Mico Davidovic has stated that he has approval by General Mladic for all these measures, which is not correct." And before that, paragraph 5 says: "After Major Micic was detained at SJB Bijeljina, he was stripped naked and started their interrogation only 90 minutes later, and later on they searched his house." Are you aware of this telegram sent by Colonel Tolimir to me and the Minister of the Interior, that you detained this major, locked him up at the police station, stripped him naked, and left him like that for 90 minutes, and then interrogated him and searched his house?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let him answer. Do not interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then give me more time, then give me enough time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I came to Bijeljina, I only had the orders of the then Minister Bulatovic that related to paramilitaries, that whoever was found looting or robbing, that they should all be taken in and prosecuted, and that the measures envisaged by law should be taken. As for the agreements about my authority, an agreement was reached with General Ratko Mladic, and he personally requested that regardless of whether the persons were active-duty officers or not, that we should take all measures envisaged by law. When someone was taken in by our police, military police would be informed about that, and this military police in Bijeljina would also take certain measures. It is true that we took in, among others, General Micic, and that for these reasons a dispatch was sent to Minister Mico Stanisic. And then Mico asked us what this was all about. I drew up a simple report for him about that, and I clarified this on several occasions when I was a witness in the Mico Stanisic trial, and during the preparation for my testimony, I discussed the details mentioned here. What was this about? Dusko Atanackovic, who was the chief of security of the corps in Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry. I believe you allow the Prosecution to control and lead the examination. This is too long a story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you arrested this man, stripped him naked, and whether you were ordered to do this by Pavle Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an order from Ratko Mladic to take in and detain military personnel, and if I did that, that I should inform military police about that and military authorities, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mladic tell you to strip them naked?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told them to strip them naked, nor were they stripped naked. But when they are taken in, then their belt would be taken off, and their shoelaces, so that they wouldn't commit suicide. There was no reason for them to be stripped naked. There are such claims, but they have nothing to do with truth. However, anyone has the right to claim whatever he wants. But I know what the rules are, and they were applied.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2808, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 7138, can we see that document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is in evidence as Exhibit P2895.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, to this telegram which was sent to me and Stanisic, Stanisic replies to the Security Services Centre in Bijeljina. That was probably in -- Andan at that moment in July, or it was perhaps still Jesuric. Please have a look at this document. It says that: "The Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic has informed us that special MUP units have arrested the battalion commander of the 1st Semberija Brigade, Major Jovan Micic, because of the robbery committed by six soldiers from his unit, whom you have also arrested." And then it says: "It is necessary that you immediately hand over the arrested major and his soldiers to the military police. "We emphasise, once again, as we have already done several times verbally or in directives and orders, that measures must be taken and procedures followed in a completely legal manner and the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs, the Law on Criminal Procedure, and other regulations in the field of internal affairs must be observed. And if offences are committed by military personnel, and under Articles 115, 116 and 117 of the Law on the Army, must also be observed, with full co-operation and co-ordination action with military organs in preventing and detecting crimes and their perpetrators." So could the late Pavle Bulatovic order you, and did he order you or not - you can answer with yes or no - to do anything that was outside the provisions of the Law on Interior Affairs, the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not have ordered me to do anything that was not in accordance with the law. But he emphasised that, in agreement with General Mladic, whatever was applied to civilians should also be applied to military personnel. But when active-duty military personnel were detained or taken in, it was our duty to inform military police about that, which we did. When Major Micic is mentioned here, we should emphasise that he was found while perpetrating a crime, because he had stolen goods, items, technical goods in three trucks which he was driving from Brcko to his house. That was why we conducted a search of his house with personnel from the Crime Prevention Service. We found several truckloads of stolen goods. Everything was seized and placed in the Bijeljina MUP premises.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 18364, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the same day, the 5th of July, Minister Stanisic, is writing to the Command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and in this dispatch he says that as soon as he learned that the major was arrested: "... we took measures for them to be handed over to the military police." He then says that there were many crimes committed by individuals and groups, most often armed, and as there are not enough Crime Prevention Service employees who can carry out the duties in Semberija: "... please help us to prevent the commission of the crimes and discover the perpetrators ..." And so on and so forth. He asks for co-operation, and so on and so forth. Did you know that this was addressed to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And after that, there were no such incidents anymore, because Petar Salapura, who was an envoy from the Military Security Service, from the Main Staff Command, spent quite a lot of time together with me, so that we reacted jointly. And together with the military police, we arrested military personnel and prosecuted them just like civilians. But there were no more documents like this one issued, because it was clarified, what my authority was, and what was the basis for my coming to the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that I did not respond, and do you find this normal, because the minister is working and doing his job?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mico talked to me immediately, and in another memo he indicated that there should be no such objections voiced anymore so that there would be no confrontation between us and the organs and the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1408, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 205 of your statement, you say that in your opinion, there was even an instance when your son was kidnapped. Isn't that what you say? Please have a look at paragraph 205 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that your son was kidnapped and that these were Petko Budisa and Tomo Kovac who had arranged the kidnapping of your son; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you connect that with your activities, that that was a sort of revenge against you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was revenge against me, but it was very unpleasant. They took in my son without identifying themselves and saying where they were taking him. And then at 9.00, or 9.30, rather, they called me to my office at the Belgrade SUP. My wife called me and his wife, my son's wife, and they told me that, Last night, Jovica had been taken away, this son of mine. I tried to establish who had taken him from Kijac, from Drago Vukovic, from -- I don't know who else I asked. Nobody could tell me if he had been taken, and where, and if these were legal organs. And around 11.00, an inspector from Bijeljina called me on the phone and told me, You have to know that now is the time when people are taken away from their homes at night and murdered, so you can expect anything. It's even possible that your child may be found dead somewhere. You can imagine what sort of shock a man experiences when he's told that his child has gone missing, and that he can expect that he might be found murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your son Jovica have any problems with the law, and does he have any problems still?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What sort of problems?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was this vehicle which you mentioned. He had a vehicle which he had bought from a person. He also had a traffic license in his name. And when this was seized from him, I mean the vehicle, three or four days later he was sitting in front of a cafe in Bijeljina with a group of his friends, and he saw the same car passing along, being driven by somebody else and with different license plates. So with a group of his friends who were present, he went -- or, rather, the vehicle was next to Dvori, and in front of the Spaj, in front of the hotel in Dvori, he went out with a gun in his hand. He took the vehicle. He said it was his, and he drove it away and put it in a garage somewhere, intending to hide it. Then a procedure was initiated, and they said that this was a crime of robbery. As far as I know, later on during the proceedings, he was acquitted for that part and he was released from custody, and this is what I know about these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he have any other problems with the law?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had another one two or three years ago. I don't know what it was. It had to do with a conflict with some persons. He was --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Objection. I question the relevance of this kind of issue. I mean, the witness has mentioned the event with the car, and it's sort of related to this case. But whatever the son did three years ago is not really of concern for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I quite agree with it. Mr. Karadzic, move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, if you look at paragraph 205, where the arrest -- or, rather, the taking in of this witness's son, it's connected with his activities. Let's have a look how this is phrased, this paragraph: [In English] "... The wanted to avenge everything I had done. Kijac didn't tell me who was after me. I eventually found that my son was being held at the Brcko SUP. A colleague of mine, Krsto Stojkic, from Bijeljina, was in Brcko at the time, and he was told by someone from SUP that my son was being held there." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. And then it reads that Petko Budisa, who was a high-ranking police official, and Tomo Kovac, who was a minister, had arranged his kidnapping, and today he says that he was only taken in. So this is really relevant, because the father was concerned about his son, to be sure, and this instance is important, particularly as the witness, himself, says that this was connected with his activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic, this issue is something I have to clarify. You certainly want me to do that. You're trying, in every possible way, to devalue me and my family. You use all means available, and you want to show that my son has a criminal character. Mr. Karadzic, I did very complex and difficult duties, the most difficult duties that existed at the time. When I arrested Dusko and his brother, the Yellow Wasps, and the remaining members of the gang which kidnapped and looted around Zvornik, and when these persons were prosecuted, after 30 days they were released from custody, and I will tell you, it was at your and Mr. Krajisnik's insistence, according to your theory that Serbs should not be arrested or prosecuted. And this Zuco was released from custody, and as soon as he did, on that very day, on that very moment, he went looking for my son, and then he put a Colt gun in his mouth and asked him, Where is your Daddy now? You do not mention this or other consequences that me and my family had to bear throughout the war, because when I left from Bijeljina, two times they entered into my and my parents' house. Searches were conducted because allegedly I was hiding Muslims in my house. Pressure was exerted on me. Whoever of my family members was found in the street, they were frisked. They wanted to show that they had power, and they said, "Where is this Mico Davidovic now? Can he put up any resistance now? I did not want to complain about this before this Tribunal, but you are trying to show, in every possible way, what sort of relationship I and my family had or the attitude we had towards some legal decisions, leaving aside the fact that we did many good things, that we found many perpetrators, murderers and criminals, and you should not try to devalue this and humiliate me as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Davidovic, we'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time. It's time to take a break. We'll have a break for half an hour, and when we resume at 11.00, I would like you to move on to another topic, leaving the issue of his son. 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, did you have any knowledge to the effect that I had ordered the arrest of the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I was told by Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, you said that either I or Krajisnik had ordered their release; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I or Krajisnik; who?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my information was that both you and Krajisnik intervened that they be released from detention, and that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that was done, proceedings were brought to an end?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Proceedings were never initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You had information from who?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from the judiciary and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Name, surname, time, when you received this information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by my colleague, Ostoja Minic, who was working on that case, who was writing up the criminal report, and later on I heard that at the Prosecutor's Office as well, from the prosecutor. I think her name was Nada Milosevic. I can also tell you about the details that led to the interruption in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Is this Ostoja Minic alive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he write the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on the team that was working on the criminal report. It was either Vukovic or Dragan Andan that signed the report. I think that it was Dragan who was supposed to write it because he was chief of the centre then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it you? Didn't you write up the criminal report after carrying out the appropriate procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrested the Yellow Wasps, and they were brought into custody, and they were disarmed, if I can put it that way. That is how I eliminated them as a paramilitary formation. And the professional services within the organ of the interior were in charge of their own work. Some people are involved in identification, others in taking statements, and also the preparations for writing up the criminal report. These are teams that are involved in all of this. If I were to be involved in arrests and writing of criminal reports and everything, then I'd probably have to be working 100 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just yes or no, did you state on several occasions that you had processed them and that you wrote the criminal report? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did take part in their processing and in the preparation of the criminal report, but -- I was present as they were being interviewed, but I did not write the criminal report. I had actually left when the criminal report was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you also to pause between question and answer. Now I'm going to mention some names to keep things short. Did you know some of these persons, and were you also opponents with persons like Vojislav Jekic, Goran Zugic, Mauzer, Dusko Malovic? Did you know these people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were all of them killed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Vojislav Jekic was killed, as far as I know, somewhere in Belgrade. Vojkan Djurkovic is alive. Mauzer was killed, also after the war. I don't know exactly when. That is in response to the questions that you've put.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I mentioned Vojkan Djurkovic. I probably meant Goran Zugic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, Goran. He was killed later in Montenegro, when we were working on Operation Zvornik, a few months later he went to Zvornik, and he was the chief of the Security Centre in Herceg Novi, then he was transferred to the MUP and allegedly he was killed there. I don't know what happened, and how this happened, but that is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So they were not killed in combat. They were killed criminally, in the street or somewhere else, Mauzer, Vojislav Jekic, Goran Zugic, and Dusko Malovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were killed, but I know that Jekic was killed in Belgrade, when he was leaving a car. Mauzer was killed in Bijeljina, when he was in a vehicle. I don't know where and how Zugic was killed. I just know I heard that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The six-member group of your son, were they accused of murdering Mauzer, and was one of them found?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The group of your son, consisting of six men, was it suspected of having committed that murder, and was one of them found guilty as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saying that it's a group that includes my son, I think that that is totally improper. Now, whether he was interviewed in connection with the Mauzer case, you, again, have to ask him. The man is 40 years old. You can talk to him. I don't know. I must admit that I do not have much communication with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that you did not know that your son was a suspect in Mauzer's assassination?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a suspect, and please do not present these untruths. I know a detail that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic raises here quite some very serious allegations, and he just puts it like this. That's not proper. If he wants to -- if he wants to say something about the witness or his family is responsible for killing opponents - it seems to me that's what he's heading to - he should actually have something in hand to do that and not just raise these kind of allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So far, the witness has been able to answer the questions, so I let it go. Probably he's going to put something to the witness. Did you like to say something more, Mr. Davidovic, when I interrupted you? Please carry on. You said your son was not a suspect. Otherwise, I will have Mr. Karadzic continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is truly improper to say that he was a suspect. That is untrue, and I think that this is no accident, that they were trying to link him to that. And I think it had to do with me, actually. Ever since I appeared before this Court, they have been trying to involve me and my son in different ways to show that I was a man who testified in The Hague, and they're trying to portray me as an unreliable witness. The facts that Mr. Karadzic has been stating in relation to suspicions regarding my son, I have to repeat, once again, are total rubbish. There was this big article that appeared one day that said that my son took part in Mauzer's murder directly. An investigation was conducted, and I didn't want to interfere in any way. And the investigation concluded that he had nothing to do with it. The person who had perpetrated that crime was arrested. Another person who also participated in this had allegedly been killed earlier on, and that is what I know. Now, bringing my son up now and linking him up to all of this is truly unfair, but he is probably trying to challenge everything that I've been saying, and that is the reason why he is putting these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, is it correct that Mauzer was killed in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at all when he was killed, the date or the day, or was I interested in that, when he was killed or why he was killed. I'm just saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was killed on the 7th of June, 2000, and you testified against Krajisnik in June 2005; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what does that have to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I have any interest in doing so, we're going to go back to that, but this is what I'm putting to you, Mr. Davidovic, as you say this is a generally-known proposition: As you were trying to save your son because Mauzer's murderer was in his group of six men and he was a suspect, you resorted to extremely false testimony before this Court in order to make things easier for your son. That is my proposition, not what you said, that your son had difficulties on account of your testifying, because you testified in 2005, and Mauzer was killed in 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could both speakers be asked to speak slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Davidovic, the witness, denied his son being a member of those alleged -- a group of six men and also denied that his son was a suspect. In order to put that question to the witness again, you need to put something that would support your allegation. And when you -- I would like both of you to slow down and put a pause between the question and answer. So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it is correct that Mr. Davidovic is challenging the fact that his son was a suspect, and that he was a member of the six persons that included the murderer, I would like to ask for this text to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, indeed, this is the first time I hear these questions from you. I have been through this entire procedure of giving a statement, and then I came to The Hague a couple of days ago. No one ever, especially not this Office of the Prosecutor, and I'm referring to everyone that I spoke to, no one ever mentioned this and no one ever mentioned my son in any way in relation to my testimony. As a matter of fact, I am 100 per cent certain that this OTP, in addition to the fact that this is the third time that I am appearing before this Court, never had any knowledge or any motive, or they never talked to me about my son in any way, especially not in the context of Mauzer's assassination. I think that they, themselves, are taken aback by what is being said here, and bringing me into this context and saying that I was blackmailed to say something to your detriment and in the interest of the OTP. I think that is so improper and that it goes way beyond any kind of elementary propriety. I think that this kind of behaviour on your part is totally inappropriate, and in the future I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to spare me of this kind of polemic with you. Obviously, you are moving on to a topic that has nothing to do with my testimony, and I presented 90 per cent of all of this in my statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this please be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, may I remind you of the fact that I did not involve your son. You involved your son.
